Volume I · Source section 52 of 105

S07 | RPD design: applying the sequence

F Pros Chapter 6 → Diploma Unit 6

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.2–2c.6, 2c.13, 2c.20

CORE PRINCIPLE

Start from the saddle and support; only then choose clasps, connector and indirect retention.

01 Design in order

Saddles → support → retention → bracing/reciprocation → major connectors → indirect retention → review. Identify Kennedy class after extractions; a distal-extension RPD needs tooth-and-mucosa support.

02 Biomechanical consequences

Mesial rests and stress-releasing concepts may reduce torque on distal-extension abutments. Survey casts, establish the insertion path and create suitable guide planes and rest seats before taking the definitive impression.

03 Numbers worth interpreting

The F Pros source gives a common 0.25 mm Co-Cr undercut and approximately 0.5 mm for cast gold/wrought wire. A lingual bar generally needs adequate functional sulcus depth, approximately 7–8 mm between the gingival margin and floor of mouth; otherwise consider a lingual plate.

04 Common failures

Pain after fitting may arise from overextension, tissue pressure or a high rest seat. Distal-extension saddles lose support as the ridge changes; assess the need for reline rather than merely tightening a clasp.

05 Exam trap

A retentive clasp without effective reciprocation is not a complete design. Choosing a clasp before assessing support and insertion path reverses the design logic.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Framework design must be individualized to teeth, anatomy and support; numerical rules are approximate.

Source material: F Pros pp. 21–23 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Volume I · Source section 53 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 6: RPD biomechanics: support before clasp retention

RPD biomechanics: support before clasp retention

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

For a distal-extension saddle, the support tissues move differently: tooth-supported rests resist displacement, while mucosa can compress and rotate the base.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Kennedy Class I/II free-end saddleDifferential tooth and tissue displacementBroad base coverage, mesial rests and controlled stress release
Short distal base and terminal clasp on tilted toothLevering increases load on abutmentResurvey path, rests, guide planes and clasp design
Deep undercut on weak or highly mobile abutmentRetentive force may be excessive Reduce demand or redesign with indirect retention/support
Long-span major connector or flexible baseFlexure compromises distribution and reciprocationProvide adequate rigidity, hygiene and clearance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The framework should resist displacement towards tissues (rests and base), away from tissues (retentive arm and indirect retention), and laterally (bracing and reciprocation). A retentive clasp is not an adequate substitute for properly placed rests and a rigid major connector.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A Kennedy I patient repeatedly loosens a clasp after adding a thin distal acrylic saddle. The first priority is not a stiffer clasp: assess extension, support, rotation axis, rest position and occlusion.

EXAM TRAP

In a free-end saddle, an excessively rigid distal clasp can torque the abutment during tissueward movement.

Volume I · Source section 54 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 6: Altered-cast impression: procedure and indication

Altered-cast impression: procedure and indication

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The altered-cast technique aims to record the distal-extension mucosa under a selected functional condition while preserving the tooth-supported framework relationship.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Indication: distal-extension RPDTooth and mucosal support are dissimilarConsider altered cast where clinically useful and technically feasible
Framework trial before final impressionStable rests and complete seating requiredVerify passivity, rests, guide planes and occlusal clearance
Custom tray attached to seated frameworkAccurate impression of saddle-bearing tissuesBorder mould, apply chosen impression technique and control pressure
Master cast modified after impressionDistal saddle section replaced using secured frameworkReseat framework precisely; pour altered section without displacement

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Sequence: make accurate master cast; survey/design and fabricate Co-Cr framework; verify full framework seating intraorally; attach/assess saddle trays; border-mould and record tissues with framework held in position; section the original edentulous cast portions; seat the framework and impression on remaining tooth portions; box and pour new saddle anatomy.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

If the framework itself rocks on the rests at trial, an altered cast will reproduce a false relationship. Correct the framework or its cast before attempting to compensate with impression material.

EXAM TRAP

This is not simply "a mucocompressive impression": pressure distribution, tray relief and correct framework seating remain essential.

Volume I · Source section 55 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 6: Flexible RPD versus sectional denture

Flexible RPD versus sectional denture

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The selection should solve the anatomical insertion problem while retaining adequate support, hygiene and future adjustability.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Severe single-sided undercut prevents conventional insertionSectional denture with planned joining mechanismSelect when segments can seat on distinct paths and be stabilised
Mild undercuts and high aesthetic demandPotential indication for flexible polymer base/claspEvaluate support, replaceability, repair and tissue loading
Bilateral lingual tori with poor lingual connector clearanceConsider surgical modification or labial/sublingual alternativeDo not force a lingual bar over the tori
Lingually tilted posterior teeth obstruct insertionSurvey interference and path before deciding denture typeModify design/teeth if justified rather than defaulting to flexible

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Flexible polyamide is not equivalent to a sectional denture. A sectional design is selected for a controlled two-part insertion/removal pathway when a one-piece framework cannot be safely inserted; its attachments and stability may be technique-sensitive. Flexible bases may mask insertion issues but often offer less rigid support and more difficult modification.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A lower arch has missing anterior teeth and severely lingually inclined posterior teeth. Evaluate survey lines, guiding surfaces and the intended path first. Only if a single insertion path is not feasible should a sectional option enter the leading choices.

EXAM TRAP

A flexible denture without rest support can direct repeated tissueward force onto the residual ridge.

Volume I · Source section 56 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 6: Co-Cr RPD laboratory sequence and failure localisation

Co-Cr RPD laboratory sequence and failure localisation

REMOVABLE PARTIAL DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

The laboratory procedure board must connect clinical design with fabrication quality controls.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Survey and prescription Path of insertion, blockout and rest seats define designIdentify undercuts and components before sending to laboratory
Duplicate and refractory cast Expansion/accuracy must suit Co-Cr frameworkCheck impression duplication and refractory investment integrity
Wax pattern, sprues and castingPorosity, incomplete fill or distortion can developInspect critical connectors, clasps, rests and casting surfaces
Finishing, polishing and framework try-inOvergrinding changes strength and retentionVerify passive seating, rest contact, reciprocation and tissue clearance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

There is no single universally highest-failure step: errors can occur at impression, block-out, pattern handling, spruing, investment, burnout, casting or finishing. Distinguish a framework that does not fit the master cast (laboratory issue) from one that fits the cast but not the patient (cast/impression or clinical change).

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A Co-Cr clasp tip is short and poorly formed while the rest and connector fit: suspect local casting or finishing. A framework whose rests all fail to seat intraorally despite perfect cast fit: reassess impression and master-cast accuracy.

EXAM TRAP

Ask the technician to document alloy, casting method and repairability; never adjust a connector until design and fit have been checked.

Unit 7: Complete dentures

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 30

Retention is physics, stability is the neutral zone, and OVD is RVD minus about 3 mm.

IN ONE MINUTE

Special trays 2 mm short, border moulded; post-dam along the vibrating line.

Record the horizontal relation in RCP; the Gothic arch apex marks it.

Every post-insertion complaint maps to a flange, the seal, the occlusion or the OVD.

7.3 Record blocks and the occlusal plane

Upper rim: labial face supports the lip; the labial surfaces of the central incisors usually lie about 8–10 mm anterior to the centre of the incisive papilla.

Upper incisal level: about 1–2 mm of rim visible below the relaxed upper lip in younger patients; less with age.

Occlusal plane parallel to the interpupillary line anteriorly and to the ala–tragal line (Camper's plane) posteriorly; checked with

a Fox's plane guide.

Lower posterior occlusal plane at about two-thirds the height of the retromolar pad and level with the lateral border of the tongue at rest.

Centre line coincides with the facial midline (philtrum); canine lines at the corners of the mouth at rest; high lip (smile) line shows the necessary length of the teeth.

7.5 Horizontal jaw relation

Complete dentures are made in the retruded contact position (RCP) because it is reproducible; ICP is coincident with it in the finished dentures.

7.6 Articulators and occlusion

Simple hinge: no lateral movement, ignore.

Average value: fixed condylar guidance (about 30°) and Bonwill triangle (about 10 cm sides); adequate for most complete dentures.

Semi-adjustable (arcon or non-arcon): condylar guidance set from a protrusive record; Bennett angle often from Hanau's

formula L = H/8 + 12; used with a facebow.

Arcon: condylar element on the lower member, anatomically correct (Whip Mix, Denar). Non-arcon: condylar element on the

upper member (Dentatus, Hanau H2).

Facebow: records the relationship of the maxillary arch to the hinge axis (arbitrary or kinematic), so arcs of closure on the articulator match the patient's.

Christensen's phenomenon: separation of posterior teeth (or rims) in protrusion because the condyles move down the

eminence. Bilateral balanced occlusion requires a compensating curve.

Hanau's quint: condylar guidance, incisal guidance, cusp angle, plane of orientation, compensating curve.

Balanced (bilateral) occlusion: simultaneous contacts on working and non-working sides in excursion — keeps complete dentures stable.

Volume I · Source section 59 of 105

Unit 7: Complete dentures

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 32

Lingualised occlusion: only upper palatal cusps contact the lower central fossae; good stability with resorbed ridges and acceptable aesthetics.

Monoplane (zero-degree) teeth: least horizontal force; for severely resorbed ridges, Class III relationships, poor neuromuscular control.

7.7 Tooth selection and setting

Anterior width: canine lines and inter-alar width; central incisor width about one-sixteenth of bizygomatic width (Berry). Williams' face-form theory and Frush and Fisher's dentogenics (sex, personality, age) guide shape but are weakly evidence-

based.

Shade: darker and with characterisation for older patients; involve the patient; avoid very light "denture look".

Lower posterior teeth over the ridge crest and in the neutral zone; never on the ascending slope of the ramus (the denture would be pushed forward).

Upper posterior teeth may sit buccal to a resorbed maxillary ridge; set in crossbite where the maxilla is much narrower than

the mandible.

Neutral zone: area where tongue forces balance lip and cheek forces; record with tissue conditioner, impression compound or soft wax on a lower base during function (swallowing, speaking). Most useful for resorbed lower ridges and previously unstable lower dentures.

Posterior horizontal overlap (buccal overjet) prevents cheek biting.

A clinical remount (new RCP record on the processed dentures, remounted on the articulator) corrects occlusal errors from processing more accurately than adjusting in the mouth.

7.10 Special complete denture techniques

Copy (replica) dentures: duplicate the polished and occlusal surfaces of dentures the patient has adapted to, changing only what is necessary (fitting surface, OVD, occlusion). Best for older patients with poor adaptive capacity. The replica (wax teeth on shellac or acrylic base) acts as special tray and record block.

Immediate dentures: flanged (better retention, stability and reline potential) vs open-face (socketed; better emergence appearance but poor retention and cannot be relined labially). Teeth are removed from the cast and the sockets lightly trimmed. Leave in for the first 24 hours; review next day; reline at about 3–6 months; replace later as resorption continues.

Overdentures: retained roots (canines are ideal — longest roots, strategic position) reduced to 2–3 mm above the gingiva with domed surfaces and root fillings; preserve bone and proprioception, improve support, retention with attachments. Risks: caries and periodontitis — fluoride gel in the denture fitting surface, meticulous hygiene.

Implant overdentures: McGill consensus (2002) and York consensus (2009): a two-implant mandibular overdenture should be

the minimum standard of care for the edentulous mandible.

Single complete denture against natural teeth: risk of fracture and of combination syndrome (Kelly): anterior maxillary resorption and flabby ridge, tuberosity enlargement, papillary hyperplasia, over-eruption of lower anteriors, resorption under lower free-end saddles. Prevent by restoring posterior support (lower RPD) and reducing anterior loading.

Flabby ridge impressions: mucostatic (impression plaster) or selective pressure (windowed special tray: mucocompressive material for the firm ridge, then low-viscosity material or plaster through the window over the flabby tissue).

Reline (new fitting surface) vs rebase (whole base replaced). Chairside hard reline is quick but more porous; closed-mouth

laboratory reline can increase OVD if the patient bites too firmly.

Pre-prosthetic surgery (tuberosity reduction, vestibuloplasty, torus removal) is usually Level 3.

Examiner traps — Unit 7

Clicking teeth and generalised soreness mean the OVD is too high.

An upper denture that drops on wide opening points to the distobuccal flange and the coronoid.

The occlusal plane is parallel to the interpupillary line anteriorly and to Camper's plane posteriorly.

The two-implant overdenture is the minimum standard for the edentulous mandible.

Volume I · Source section 61 of 105

S08 | Complete dentures: stability and adaptation

F Pros Chapter 6 → Diploma Unit 7

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.4, 2c.9, 2c.13, 2c.19, 2c.21–2c.27

CORE PRINCIPLE

Retention is only one part of success: harmony with the neutral zone and the patient’s adaptation is equally important.

01 Clinical sequence

Primary impressions → special trays → border-moulded secondary impressions → occlusal rims and jaw registration → trial dentures → insertion → review. Recheck each step instead of hoping the technician will compensate for a faulty record.

02 Choose an impression strategy

Displace flabby tissue as little as clinically appropriate; selective pressure or a window technique may help. Functional borders and the posterior palatal seal have to be assessed clinically.

03 Occlusal scheme and OVD

The source summarises OVD as rest vertical dimension minus roughly 2–4 mm of freeway space. In severely resorbed ridges, lingualised or carefully balanced occlusion and a neutral-zone approach may improve stability.

04 Patient adaptation

For older patients with successful old dentures, copy techniques preserve useful adaptation while changing only identified defects. Explain the likely need for early relines with immediate dentures and the adjustment period following insertion.

05 Exam trap

Increasing vertical dimension or adding more adhesive rarely cures an overextended flange, inaccurate border, unstable record or incorrect neutral-zone position.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Discuss implant-assisted dentures as an option or referral; specialist implant surgery is not a Level 2 learning requirement.

Source material: F Pros pp. 21–23 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Volume I · Source section 62 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 7: Flabby and atrophic ridges: functional impression choice

Flabby and atrophic ridges: functional impression choice

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

An impression should preserve tissue form and record useful support without displacing tissue that rebounds after insertion.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Mobile anterior maxillary ridge Selective pressure/window or mucostatic recordingMinimise distortion over flabby area; use stable palate for support
Flat mandibular ridge with limited attached mucosaFunctionally shaped borders and broad supportAssess retromylohyoid and buccal shelf before increasing OVD
Denture sore spots despite good static fitDynamic border overextension or occlusal traumaMap pressure under functional movements
Rigid impression material in deep undercutsRemoval trauma and distortion riskChoose appropriate elastomer or block out as indicated

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Mucostatic approaches record tissue with minimal displacement; mucocompressive approaches intentionally load selected tissues; selective-pressure approaches combine support and relief. No single impression material alone guarantees the physiological pressure state - tray design and operator control matter.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

An upper complete denture is unstable because mobile anterior ridge tissue was compressed during the wash impression. A windowed or selective-pressure technique is preferable to simply increasing posterior palatal seal pressure.

EXAM TRAP

Do not confuse an under-extended lingual flange with a need for a longer occlusal vertical dimension.

Volume I · Source section 63 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 7: Neutral zone, jaw relations and vertical dimension

Neutral zone, jaw relations and vertical dimension

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

A jaw-registration number is a cross-check, not a substitute for repeatable mandibular positioning and evaluation of facial comfort.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Severely resorbed lower ridge, unstable trial rimMuscle balance can dominate denture stabilityRecord neutral zone; shape polished surface and tooth position
Altered mandibular posture or neuromuscular diseaseRVD and repeatability can be unreliableUse several methods and patient-specific reproducibility checks
Excessive OVD Lip strain, clicking, speaking difficulty, muscle fatigueRecheck jaw relation and interocclusal rest space
Insufficient OVD Overclosure, reduced facial support and altered functionVerify before raising the bite; consider existing adaptation

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The conventional rest space is approximately 2-4 mm in many patients but varies individually. Record and verify centric relation, interocclusal distance, phonetics, facial support and comfort; copy records may help when adaptation is poor. Neutral-zone recording can be done with mouldable material over a stable base while the patient swallows and speaks.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A new lower denture repeatedly dislodges during speech despite a well-fitting base on a flat ridge. Reassess tooth position and polished-surface contour within the neutral zone before proposing an implant solely because the ridge is flat.

EXAM TRAP

A single RVD minus a fixed 3-mm value is not a sufficient method to prescribe OVD for every patient.

Volume I · Source section 64 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 7: Try-in: phonetics, facial planes and bite checks

Try-in: phonetics, facial planes and bite checks

COMPLETE DENTURES

CORE PRINCIPLE

Try-in is the point to test the proposed tooth position and jaw relation against speech, aesthetics, comfort and mandibular movement.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
F and V sounds; upper incisal edgesIncisal edges relate to the lower lip wet-dry borderAdjust length and labiolingual position, not just shade
Sibilants and closest speaking spaceExcess contact or large gap can indicate errorCheck anterior relation and vertical dimension together
Occlusal plane wax rim Facial plane references aid orientationUse interpupillary line/frontal aesthetics and ala-tragus as guides
Frankfort horizontal (porion-orbitale)Reference in cephalometry and facebow orientationNot a direct stand-alone rule for denture tooth positions

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Use multiple recordings when the patient cannot repeat jaw closure: stable bases, tracing where indicated, guided closure and assessment of existing dentures. Verify centric contacts and excursions; document any deliberate changes to the established occlusion. Speech tests should use the patient's normal language and conversational rate.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A trial denture looks acceptable but S sounds whistle and the teeth contact during speaking. The more useful response is to check anterior tooth position and closest speaking space, not immediately reduce posterior cusps.

EXAM TRAP

The Frankfort horizontal reference does not replace chairside checks of smile line, occlusal plane and lip support.

Unit 8: Fixed prosthodontics

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 34

Taper, height and ferrule hold a crown on; Ante's law and the cube of the span decide a bridge.

IN ONE MINUTE

Margins supragingival where possible, and at least 3 mm from the bone crest.

For sound abutments with good enamel, a resin-bonded cantilever is the first choice.

In ceramic connectors, height matters more than width.

Fixed bridge design was examined last sitting: be fluent in abutment evaluation, choosing between fixed-fixed, cantilever, fixed-movable and resin-bonded designs, pontic forms and the mechanics of span and connectors.

8.1 Principles of tooth preparation (Shillingburg)

Preservation of tooth structure (and pulp).

Retention and resistance form.

Structural durability of the restoration (adequate material thickness, functional cusp bevel).

Marginal integrity.

Preservation of the periodontium.

Taper (total occlusal convergence): theoretical ideal about 6°; clinically 10–20° is typical and acceptable. Retention falls sharply as convergence increases.

Minimum axial wall height: about 3 mm for incisors and premolars, 4 mm for molars. Height-to-width ratio of at least 0.4

improves resistance.

Short or over-tapered preparations: add grooves or boxes, increase surface area, use adhesive cements, consider crown lengthening (Level 3 surgery) or elective endodontics with a core only as a last resort.

Pulp protection: sharp burs, copious water spray, light intermittent pressure, avoid desiccation, well-fitting temporaries;

dentine sealing.

8.2 Reduction guide

RESTORATION AXIAL OCCLUSAL / INCISAL MARGIN

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 35

Functional (supporting) cusps: palatal of upper and buccal of lower posteriors; give them a functional cusp bevel.

and aesthetics, test the planned shape, OVD or occlusion.

Materials: bis-acryl composite (low exotherm, good strength, common); PMMA (stronger for long-term but exothermic and higher residual monomer); prefabricated polycarbonate or metal crowns.

Use eugenol-free temporary cement if the definitive restoration will be resin-bonded.

8.5 Occlusion, shade and impressions

Conformative approach (most single units and short bridges): restore to the existing ICP without changing the occlusal

scheme.

Reorganised approach (RCP/centric relation): when ICP is unstable, extensive restoration is planned, or OVD will change.

Usually Level 3 when major.

Shade: take before preparation (teeth dehydrate and lighten during treatment), in colour-corrected daylight, quickly; value is the most important dimension; photograph with shade tabs and send to the laboratory.

Impressions: addition silicone or polyether in a rigid tray; dual-arch (triple) trays only for single units with stable intercuspation. Intraoral scans suit short-span work.

Die spacer (about 20–40 µm) gives room for cement; it stops short of the margin.

8.6 Endodontically treated teeth

Posterior root-filled teeth need cuspal coverage (onlay or crown) — survival improves markedly (Sorensen and Martinoff); anterior root-filled teeth with little tissue loss can be restored with composite.

Ferrule of 1.5–2 mm of sound dentine is the most important factor in fracture resistance (Section 3.13 for post rules).

Posts retain cores; they do not strengthen roots.

Molars: amalgam or composite core retained in the pulp chamber (Nayyar core) without a post is often enough.

Provide a good coronal seal promptly after root canal treatment; coronal leakage contributes to failure.

8.7 Bridge terminology and abutment evaluation

Terms: abutment (supporting tooth), retainer (restoration on the abutment), pontic (replacement tooth), connector (joint), span, unit.

Abutment assessment: periodontal health and bone support, crown–root ratio (ideally 2:3, minimum 1:1), root form (divergent multi-rooted and long roots are better than conical or fused), root surface area, mobility, pulpal and endodontic status,

Volume I · Source section 67 of 105

Unit 8: Fixed prosthodontics

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 36

restorative condition, position and angulation, opposing occlusion.

Ante's law: the total root surface area of the abutments should equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced. It is historical and not well supported by evidence, but still examined.

Relative root surface area (largest to smallest): maxilla 6 > 7 > 3 > 4 ≈ 5 > 1 > 2; mandible 6 > 7 > 3 > 5 ≈ 4 > 2 > 1. Upper canine has the largest root of the single-rooted teeth.

Span mechanics: deflection of a beam increases with the cube of its length and decreases with the cube of its thickness (occluso-gingival connector height). Doubling the span gives about eight times the flexure.

Arch curvature: pontics lying outside the line joining the abutments (e.g., replacing all four upper incisors) act as a lever arm causing torque.

Pier abutment: a rigid five-unit bridge with a pier tooth risks debonding of a terminal retainer because the pier acts as a fulcrum. Use a non-rigid connector (keyway on the distal of the pier retainer) or separate bridges.

8.9 Resin-bonded bridges in detail

Advantages: minimal or no preparation, no anaesthesia, reversible, cheap, quick; pulp not at risk; failures usually rebondable.

Requirements: sound abutment with large enamel area, adequate occlusal clearance for the wing (about 0.7 mm Co-Cr or Ni-

Cr) or a Dahl approach, stable occlusion.

Design features: maximum wing coverage of enamel within aesthetic limits, wraparound (about 180°), occlusal or cingulum

rests, minimal preparation (rest seats, guide planes) to define the path and resistance.

Bonding: air-abrade the metal (50 µm alumina), MDP-containing resin cement (e.g., Panavia) for base metals; rubber dam; etch

enamel.

Pontic tissue surface: convex, smooth and glazed porcelain or highly polished metal; never pressing on the mucosa (blanching) in fixed work.

Narrow the buccolingual width of posterior pontics to reduce load.

8.11 Connectors and all-ceramic bridges

Connectors are the weakest point of all-ceramic bridges. Approximate minimum cross-sections: lithium disilicate 12 mm²

anterior and 16 mm² premolar (3-unit maximum, not beyond the second premolar); zirconia about 9 mm² for 3-unit posterior

and more for longer spans.

Height matters more than width: connector strength rises with the square of height; deflection falls with the cube.

Open gingival embrasures in connectors aid hygiene; rounded connector radii reduce stress concentration.

8.12 Veneers, onlays and inlays

Porcelain veneer indications: discolouration not responsive to bleaching, minor malalignment, diastema closure, shape change, minor fractures.

Contraindications: inadequate enamel, bruxism or heavy occlusion, edge-to-edge or Class III incisor relationship, poor oral

hygiene, heavily restored teeth.

Designs: window (no incisal involvement), feathered incisal, butt joint, incisal overlap (palatal finish line — most common for stress distribution and seating).

Bond with HF-etched, silanated ceramic and light-cured resin cement on etched enamel.

Onlays: cusp coverage for teeth with weakened cusps (cusp width less than about half its height); adhesive onlays preserve more tooth than crowns.

Inlay cavities diverge occlusally (about 6–10°) for a path of withdrawal; no undercuts.

8.13 Laboratory communication and regulation

The prescription is a legal document: patient identifier, clinician details, materials, design, shade, margin, pontic form, connector type, delivery date.

Custom-made devices fall under the UK Medical Devices Regulations: the laboratory provides a statement of manufacture; the

manufacturer must be registered with the MHRA. Retain records.

Dental technicians and clinical dental technicians are GDC registrants with their own scope of practice.

S09 | Fixed prosthodontics: preparation to review

F Pros Chapter 5 → Diploma Unit 8

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.2, 2c.4, 2c.6, 2c.11, 2c.13–2c.14

CORE PRINCIPLE

Preserve sound tooth structure and select a restoration with adequate retention, resistance and long-term hygiene.

01 Preparation principles

Compare partial coverage, onlay/overlay, resin-bonded bridge and full crown. Verify clearance, marginal design, axial wall height, taper and ferrule rather than treating one preparation number as a universal rule.

02 Use the right adhesive chemistry

The F Pros notes contrast silica-based ceramics requiring silane-based bonding with zirconia requiring alternative surface conditioning/MDP approaches. A cement cannot compensate for poor resistance form.

03 Biological protection

Deep reduction, heat, desiccation and provisional leakage can damage the pulp. Subgingival overcontours and poor emergence profiles increase plaque retention and soft-tissue inflammation.

04 Bridge design choices

Review span, abutment periodontal support, tooth preservation, patient cleaning ability and the feasibility of a cantilever resin-bonded design. More retainers are not automatically safer.

05 Success is more than survival

At recall inspect biological health, contacts, margins, caries, cracks, occlusion, aesthetics and patient satisfaction. Parafunction may change material and maintenance choices.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Full-mouth reconstruction and complex occlusal reorganisation are Level 3/referral scenarios, not routine Diploma execution.

Source material: F Pros pp. 18–20 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Volume I · Source section 71 of 105

S10 | Aesthetic dentistry: least invasive first

F Pros Chapter 10 → Diploma Unit 8

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.16 · 2b.6, 2b.10 · 2c.4

CORE PRINCIPLE

Start with a systematic assessment of the smile, then solve the patient’s actual concern using the least destructive option.

01 Analyse from outside inward

Facial symmetry and midline → lip support/smile line → incisal display and occlusal plane → tooth proportions, shade, gingival contour and papillae. A mathematical “golden proportion” is not a mandatory natural smile rule.

02 Treatment ladder

For colour: investigate aetiology and consider whitening first. For white spots: consider infiltration or microabrasion. For spacing or peg laterals: consider additive composite; for malalignment: orthodontics before elective tooth preparation.

03 Before an indirect veneer

Use diagnostic wax-up/mock-up, assess enamel availability, parafunction and deep overbite, and discuss irreversibility and long-term replacement. Whitening may alter the final shade and immediate resin bonding conditions.

04 Patient-centred consent

Discuss maintenance, failure, costs and reasonable alternatives including no treatment. Distinguish a realistic restorative concern from expectations that cannot safely be met.

05 SBA trap

A crown on an otherwise healthy tooth for a minor aesthetic complaint is generally less conservative than whitening, orthodontics or additive composite if those can meet the objective.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Complex gingival/orthognathic procedures require appropriate specialist assessment, not Diploma-level operative detail.

Crown margin and reduction: material-specific reasoning

FIXED PROSTHODONTICS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Preparation is determined by restorative material thickness, finish-line compatibility, available tooth structure and periodontal health.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Metal-ceramic/PFM crown: porcelain-bearing surfaceAdequate reduction and rounded support neededOften a shoulder/heavy chamfer for porcelain; material-specific design
Metal-only margin Conservative chamfer may be suitableAvoid under-reduction and thin unsupported metal
Glass-ceramic adhesive restorationRounded internal geometry and adequate ceramic bulkFollow ceramic and bonding system requirements
Knife-edge/feather-edge finish linePotentially appropriate for selected metal situationsPoor choice for ceramics needing identifiable bulk; difficult control

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Indicative figures differ between systems: many conventional metal-ceramic preparations use approximately 1.2-1.5 mm on porcelain-bearing axial surfaces and 1.5-2 mm occlusally/incisally where porcelain is present; monolithic materials may permit other dimensions. Use the selected manufacturer's values, not an exam-wide universal number.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A short clinical crown has limited axial wall height but is being prepared for a ceramic PFM margin. Improving resistance form and preserving sound tissue may be more important than automatically extending a deep subgingival shoulder.

EXAM TRAP

A biologic tissue attachment violation cannot be corrected simply by polishing the margin or prescribing chlorhexidine.

Volume I · Source section 73 of 105

Edition 2 | Unit 8: Retention, resistance and bridge failure

Retention, resistance and bridge failure

FIXED PROSTHODONTICS

CORE PRINCIPLE

A crown or bridge may fail despite adequate cement because the geometry cannot resist displacement or rotation.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Short, wide preparation with large taperPoor resistance to oblique displacementImprove geometry, grooves/boxes or consider alternative restorative plan
Long-span conventional bridge Deflection rises steeply with span lengthAssess abutment support, connector size, pontic position and load
Two-wing resin-bonded bridge with unilateral debondSilent caries risk under partially detached retainerConsider single-retainer cantilever and moisture/bond control
Repeated porcelain chipping on bridgeUnsupported ceramic or excursive contactReview framework support, ceramic thickness and guidance

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Retention resists withdrawal approximately along the path of insertion; resistance prevents oblique tipping/rotation. The prognosis also depends on ferrule where needed, remaining dentine, occlusal loading and periodontal status. For RBBs, enamel bonding area, rigid connector and isolation are frequently more decisive than adding another retainer.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A resin-bonded lateral-incisor replacement debonds on one of two retainers without mobility of the other. Recementing both wings without considering hidden leakage is less appropriate than redesigning the adhesive bridge and protecting abutment teeth.

EXAM TRAP

Ante's law and "span cubed" are planning prompts, not substitutes for individual bridge biomechanics.

Unit 9: Occlusion and TMD

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 39

Most TMD is myalgia: explain, self-care, simple analgesia and a hard full-arch splint, after excluding red flags.

IN ONE MINUTE

Closed lock (DDwoR) deflects the mandible to the affected side.

Canine guidance discludes all other teeth; group function shares the load on the working side.

Bruxists: hard night splint, and monolithic zirconia or metal restorations.

For TMD, the evidence-based answer is almost always reversible, conservative care first (education, self-care, a stabilisation splint); irreversible occlusal adjustment is not a treatment for TMD.

Aetiology is multifactorial (biopsychosocial): parafunction, trauma, stress, anxiety and depression, sleep disturbance, widespread pain conditions. Occlusal factors have a weak association.

TMD is commonest in women aged about 20–40.

A click without pain or locking needs no treatment beyond reassurance.

9.3 Management

Explanation and reassurance; self-limiting in most patients.

Self-care: soft diet, avoid wide opening and gum chewing, warm compresses, jaw rest, stop habits (nail biting, clenching — "lips together, teeth apart").

Simple analgesia (NSAIDs short term).

Stabilisation splint: full-coverage hard acrylic (often maxillary, Michigan type), even contacts in RCP, canine guidance, worn at night.

Physiotherapy, jaw exercises, CBT and stress management.

Referral (secondary care): persistent pain, low-dose tricyclic (by GMP or specialist), botulinum toxin, arthrocentesis, arthroscopy, surgery.

Soft splints are for short-term use (may increase clenching in some).

Anterior repositioning splints (for disc displacement with reduction) are short-term only: long-term use risks a posterior open bite.

Partial-coverage anterior bite planes can let uncovered posterior teeth over-erupt if worn continuously.

Closed lock of recent onset: manipulation to recapture the disc may be tried; otherwise reassure, splint, exercises.

Acute dislocation: reduce by pressing the mandible downwards and backwards (thumbs on the lower molars or external oblique ridges); advise limited opening.

9.4 Red flags in orofacial pain

Jaw claudication, temporal tenderness and headache over age 50: giant cell arteritis (urgent ESR/CRP, same-day medical referral — risk to vision).

Progressive trismus, numbness, unexplained weight loss, lymphadenopathy, otalgia with a normal ear, nasal obstruction:

Volume I · Source section 76 of 105

Unit 9: Occlusion and TMD

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 41

possible malignancy (nasopharyngeal, parotid, infratemporal).

Cardiac pain referred to the jaw on exertion.

Paroxysmal electric-shock pain triggered by light touch: trigeminal neuralgia (carbamazepine, via GMP or specialist).

9.5 Occlusion in restorative planning

Record and examine on mounted casts before multiple restorations; identify interferences, slide, guidance.

Conform to ICP when it is stable and comfortable; reorganise to RCP when it is not, or when OVD is changed or extensive

rehabilitation is planned.

Bruxism signs: attrition facets, fractured restorations and cusps, masseteric hypertrophy, scalloped tongue, linea alba. Protect new work with a night-time hard splint; prefer metal or monolithic zirconia occlusal surfaces over layered porcelain.

Occlusal equilibration (selective grinding) is irreversible: only to remove specific interferences for restorative reasons, not as

TMD treatment.

Examiner traps — Unit 9

Selective occlusal grinding is not an evidence-based TMD treatment.

Reduce an acute dislocation by pressing downwards and backwards.

Suspected giant cell arteritis needs same-day medical referral.

A full-time anterior repositioning splint risks a posterior open bite.

Volume I · Source section 77 of 105

S11 | TMD: diagnosis, red flags and self-care

F Pros Chapter 8 → Diploma Unit 9

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.15, 2a.20 · 2c.19

CORE PRINCIPLE

Most common TMD presentations should be assessed conservatively; not every jaw pain is TMD.

01 Classify rather than guess

Separate muscle-related pain, TMJ arthralgia and disc/displacement disorders using the history and examination; consider the DC/TMD framework. Document pain location, movement limitation, joint noise, locking and functional impact.

02 First-line management

Explain the condition, provide reassurance, self-care, soft diet during acute symptoms, habit awareness, controlled jaw exercise and appropriate analgesia. A reversible stabilisation splint may be useful in selected cases.

03 Avoid irreversible overtreatment

Occlusal adjustment, orthodontics and extensive restorative reconstructions are not default cures for TMD. Changing an otherwise stable occlusion for pain without a sound diagnosis is a common examiner trap.

04 Recognise red flags

Suspicious swelling, unexplained neurological signs, significant trauma, systemic inflammatory features, rapidly progressive restriction or atypical pain should trigger broader assessment and appropriate referral.

05 Imaging decisions

Routine imaging is not obligatory for typical uncomplicated muscle pain. Choose targeted imaging when the clinical question concerns bone pathology, structural change or an alternative diagnosis.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Persistent complex TMD, diagnostic uncertainty or closed lock not responding to conservative care is a referral issue.

Occlusion across teeth, dentures and implants

OCCLUSION AND TMD

CORE PRINCIPLE

Occlusal scheme follows the supporting system: periodontal ligament, mucosa and osseointegrated implant tissues respond differently to load.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Dentate patient with healthy periodontal supportControlled intercuspation with functional guidanceExamine excursive contacts, symptoms and restoration design
Kennedy Class I RPD opposing teethSaddle rotation under function can destabilise prosthesisCoordinate base support, balanced contacts and clasp mechanics
Bilateral complete dentures Destabilising lateral contacts and tipping are criticalSelect an appropriate balanced or lingualised scheme
Implant crown/bridge or overdentureImplants lack conventional PDL proprioceptionAvoid uncontrolled cantilever and non-axial overload; monitor hardware

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A non-working interference is not automatically pathogenic. Relate it to the patient's symptoms, wear, mobility, restorations and functional pattern. Irreversible equilibration is inappropriate as a routine primary treatment for nonspecific TMD. Bruxism may increase prosthetic complications but should not be equated with a diagnosis of TMD.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A complete denture tips during excursion on steep posterior cusps; contact adjustment may help. The same contact in a patient with natural dentition and no symptoms does not justify wholesale occlusal grinding.

EXAM TRAP

Stable occlusion is an outcome of support and anatomy, not merely a collection of articulating-paper marks.

IN ONE MINUTE

Phases: urgent → stabilisation → reassessment (50% improvement = engaging) → definitive → maintenance.

Know what is Level 2 and what is Level 3 under the NHS standard.

Decide restorability before root canal treatment.

10.1 Phased treatment planning

Urgent care: relief of pain and infection.

Stabilisation (hygiene phase): oral hygiene and diet advice, caries removal and temporisation, periodontal steps 1–2, extraction of hopeless teeth, transitional or interim prostheses, smoking cessation and medical risk control.

Reassessment: response to stabilisation, motivation (plaque and bleeding scores — a 50% improvement indicates an engaging patient), prognosis of remaining teeth.

Definitive (corrective) phase: endodontics, periodontal surgery if needed, then fixed and removable prosthodontics.

Maintenance: recall interval matched to risk; supportive periodontal care; prosthesis review.

10.2 Managing tooth wear

Identify and remove the cause (diet diary, medical history for GORD and eating disorders, habits); refer to GMP for intrinsic

causes.

Prevention: reduce frequency of acidic intake and confine it to meals, drink through a straw, do not brush immediately after acid exposure, fluoride (high-concentration toothpaste, varnish), desensitising agents, night-time splint for bruxism.

Monitor: photographs, study casts, silicone indices, BEWE or Smith and Knight scores.

Restore when there is pain or sensitivity, aesthetic or functional concern, structural compromise or pulpal risk, or documented progression despite prevention.

Minimal-intervention additive approach first: direct resin composite (repairable, adhesive, reversible), then indirect composite or gold or ceramic onlays and palatal veneers; conventional crowns last (they remove more tooth).

10.3 The Dahl concept

Origin: Dahl (1975) used a removable cobalt–chromium anterior bite platform to create space for restoring worn upper anterior

teeth; today the same principle uses direct composite restorations placed at an increased OVD.

How it works: posterior teeth are initially out of contact. Over about 4–6 months (occasionally up to 18) occlusal contacts re-establish by a combination of intrusion of the anterior teeth and over-eruption (extrusion) of the posterior teeth, with some mandibular repositioning.

Best suited to localised anterior wear where compensatory dentoalveolar growth has removed interocclusal space.

Relative contraindications: active periodontal disease, implants or ankylosed teeth in the posterior segments (cannot erupt), active TMD, anterior open bite tendency, patients on drugs that affect bone turnover (bisphosphonates), poor compliance.

Dahl approach (localised).

Increase OVD (generalised; reorganised occlusion).

Surgical crown lengthening (Level 3; risks root exposure and unfavourable crown–root ratio).

Adjust opposing teeth (minor).

Elective endodontics to gain space: avoid.

S12 | Tooth wear: prevention before rebuilding

F Pros Chapter 9 → Diploma Unit 10

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.4, 1.8 · 2a.15, 2a.20 · 2c.10–2c.12

CORE PRINCIPLE

The exam tests the causes, progression and consequences of wear—not just how to create restorative space.

01 Identify the mechanism

Erosion is acid-mediated; attrition is tooth-to-tooth contact; abrasion is friction with an external object; abfraction is a debated stress-related model. Mixed lesions are common, so identify relevant risk factors and their frequency.

02 Establish whether to intervene

Record history, photos, charting and, where useful, BEWE or serial scans/casts. Assess dentine sensitivity, aesthetics, dento-alveolar compensation, pulp risk and whether wear is active.

03 Disease control and additive care

Manage dietary acid and reflux/eating-disorder concerns, optimise fluoride measures and monitor. For suitable localised anterior wear, Dahl-type relative axial movement can help gain space with additive restorations.

04 When rehabilitation is complex

Changes in OVD, unstable occlusion, severe generalised wear, reduced crown height or multiple failing restorations require a diagnostic wax-up, temporary testing and often specialist planning.

05 SBA traps

Do not infer reduced OVD from worn teeth alone. Do not plan full crowns before stabilising the cause of erosion or reviewing the amount of remaining tooth tissue.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

This covers recognition and planning. Specialist crown lengthening/reorganisation is a referral pathway when indicated.

S13 | Trauma: prosthodontic consequences

F Pros Chapter 12 → Diploma Unit 10

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.7, 2a.9–2a.10, 2a.14, 2a.18 · 2c.10

CORE PRINCIPLE

F Pros includes a full trauma chapter; for the Diploma, focus on identification, urgent action, restorability and referral.

01 Emergency recognition

The source cites IADT 2020: replant an avulsed permanent tooth promptly if appropriate; never replant an avulsed primary tooth. If immediate replantation is not possible, preserve the tooth in an appropriate medium and arrange urgent expert care.

02 Longer-term complications

After trauma, monitor for pulpal necrosis, inflammatory or replacement resorption, ankylosis, colour changes and root fracture healing. Interpret radiographs and clinical signs together over time.

03 Plan around growth

An osseointegrated implant does not erupt with a growing jaw, so a fixed implant is generally deferred until growth is complete. Temporary tooth replacement or orthodontic options may preserve future choices.

04 Restorability principles

Consider sound tissue, root length, fracture position, periodontal support, ferrule and expected maintenance. A growing patient with complex traumatic injury merits multidisciplinary advice.

05 Limit of this supplement

Specific splint duration, repositioning techniques, pulpotomy and decoronation are treated in F Pros at specialist depth; they are not presented here as required Diploma operative competencies.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Use current IADT protocols in real emergencies and refer promptly. Trauma is contextual to the supplied Diploma outcomes.

Source material: F Pros pp. 35–36 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Edition 2 | Unit 10: Dental trauma: what changes prognosis?

Dental trauma: what changes prognosis?

TOOTH WEAR AND FAILING DENTITION

CORE PRINCIPLE

For the examination, establish dentition, maturity of the root, displacement, contamination, extra-oral dry time and pulpal status before selecting treatment.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Uncomplicated crown fracture Enamel/dentine fracture without pulp exposureProtect dentine and restore; assess for luxation
Complicated crown fracture Pulp exposure; stage of root maturity mattersConsider vital pulp therapy versus RCT by case factors
Root fracture cervical/mid/apical thirdCoronal fragment displacement and stability differReposition/splint where indicated and monitor healing
Avulsed permanent tooth Extra-oral dry time and storage medium criticalUrgent evidence-based replantation pathway; never replant primary tooth

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The IADT guidance separates fractures and luxation injuries from avulsion. Assess additional alveolar fracture, percussion, mobility and soft-tissue foreign bodies, and arrange the recommended serial reviews. Pulp testing immediately after trauma may be inconclusive and requires repeat evaluation.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

An avulsed mature permanent incisor stored dry for over an hour has a much poorer periodontal ligament prognosis than one promptly replanted after suitable storage. Both require urgent professional management, but long-term risks and counselling differ.

EXAM TRAP

A discoloured traumatised tooth is not automatically necrotic - examine sensibility trends, periapical changes and canal obliteration.

Tooth wear, cracked teeth and safe additive rehabilitation

TOOTH WEAR AND FAILING DENTITION

CORE PRINCIPLE

The choice to restore follows disease control, available space and prognosis, not tooth-wear severity alone.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Palatal erosion and acid exposureIntrinsic/extrinsic erosive process Investigate and control cause before definitive veneers
Flat matching occlusal facets with parafunctionAttrition may coexist with erosion Record baseline BEWE/photographs and functional risk
No restorative space despite short crownsDentoalveolar compensation Consider additive Dahl approach when appropriate
Isolated cusp pain on release with crackPossible incomplete cracked toothProtect cusp, assess pulp and crack extent before crown

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

A Dahl approach uses relative axial tooth movement to create interocclusal space, but requires appropriate patient selection and consent about temporary disclusion and monitoring. Crown-lengthening or tooth reduction can be alternatives with different biological costs. An asymptomatic crack without pulpal complications should not automatically receive RCT.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A 40-year-old with compensated anterior wear and stable posterior support needs conservative additive planning rather than routine full-mouth preparation. Another patient with active vomiting-related erosion requires medical liaison and prevention first.

EXAM TRAP

The absence of space is not evidence that increasing the entire OVD is always indicated.

Unit 11: Implants and digital workflows

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 45

Primary stability is mechanical, two implants are the minimum for the edentulous mandible, and peri-implantitis needs bone loss.

IN ONE MINUTE

Distances: 1.5 mm to a tooth, 3 mm between implants, 2 mm above the IAN.

Screw-retained crowns are retrievable; cement-retained crowns risk residual subgingival cement.

Guided surgery merges CBCT (DICOM) with surface scans (STL).

At Level 2 you are expected to provide and maintain simple implant-retained prostheses (single tooth, simple overdenture) and

to diagnose peri-implant disease; implant assessment, planning and placement are Level 3.

11.1 Implant fundamentals

Osseointegration (Brånemark): direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-bearing implant, with no intervening soft tissue.

Stability: primary stability is mechanical (at placement); secondary stability is biological (bone remodelling over weeks). The "stability dip" occurs about 2–4 weeks after placement.

Spacing guidelines (approximate): 1.5 mm from implant to adjacent tooth; 3 mm between implants; at least 1.5–2 mm of buccal

bone; 2 mm safety margin above the inferior alveolar canal.

Loading protocols (ITI): immediate (within 1 week), early (1 week to 2 months), conventional (after 2 months).

Connections: external hex (historic, more screw loosening), internal hex or octagon, conical (Morse taper) — better seal and stability. Platform switching (narrower abutment than implant) may reduce crestal bone loss.

Risk factors for failure and peri-implantitis: smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, history of periodontitis, poor plaque control, lack of maintenance, radiotherapy to the site, high-dose IV antiresorptives, bruxism.

Record baseline radiograph and probing depths at the time of prosthesis fitting.

Maintenance: patient-performed cleaning (interdental brushes, floss under bars), professional debridement with instruments

that do not scratch titanium, annual review.

11.4 Digital prosthodontics

Intraoral scanners: excellent for short spans and single units; accuracy (trueness and precision) falls over full arches due to stitching errors. Limitations: subgingival margins, blood and saliva, edentulous mucosa (cannot mucodisplace or border mould).

File formats: STL (surface triangles, open format, no colour), PLY or OBJ (can carry colour and texture), DICOM (CBCT and

medical imaging). Merging DICOM with STL enables guided implant surgery.

Subtractive manufacture (milling): dense, homogeneous materials (pre-polymerised PMMA, zirconia, lithium disilicate, PEEK, Co-Cr, Ti); limited by bur size for fine detail.

Additive manufacture (3D printing): stereolithography (SLA), digital light processing (DLP), selective laser melting (metals).

Uses: models, surgical guides, trays, splints, temporary crowns, printed denture bases and teeth.

Digital complete dentures: fewer visits, records stored for easy duplication, milled bases have low residual monomer and excellent fit; limitations in recording functional borders and in complex jaw relations.

Digital smile design and virtual mock-ups help communication and consent; a physical mock-up from a wax-up is still useful for patient approval.

Virtual articulators and facial scanning integrate facial references; jaw motion tracking can record dynamic occlusion.

Examiner traps — Unit 11

The stability dip falls at 2–4 weeks, as primary gives way to secondary stability.

Avoid rigidly connecting a tooth to an implant.

Intraoral scans are least accurate on mobile edentulous mucosa and long spans.

Clean titanium with instruments that do not scratch it.

S14 | Implants: planning, disease and maintenance

F Pros Chapter 7 → Diploma Unit 11

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2a.19 · 2c.2, 2c.4–2c.5, 2c.21

CORE PRINCIPLE

The Diploma emphasis is prosthodontic choices, recognition of disease and safe referral—not advanced implant surgery.

01 Prosthesis-first assessment

Identify the missing-tooth problem, desired prosthesis, smile line, available restorative space, adjacent teeth, occlusion, cleansability and patient priorities before considering implant feasibility.

02 Restorative design choices

Discuss the implications of screw-retained versus cement-retained prostheses. Screw access and retrievability can be advantages; excess subgingival cement is a recognised peri-implant inflammatory risk.

03 Detect complications

Examine peri-implant tissues, bleeding or suppuration, plaque control, restoration integrity and radiographic bone levels in context. Distinguish peri-implant mucositis from suspected peri-implantitis, document findings and arrange appropriate review/referral.

04 Long-term maintenance

Outline hygiene, supportive care, prosthesis access and implant-specific complications such as screw loosening, chipping and biological inflammation. An implant surviving in situ is not synonymous with a successful functioning restoration.

05 Do not overextend the scope

Sinus grafting, ridge augmentation, complex surgical templates, advanced full-arch implants and specialist peri-implant surgery appear in F Pros but should not be treated as routine Level 2 Diploma procedures.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Source NHS complexity chart directs complex implant planning and multidisciplinary implant-related care to Level 3.

Source material: F Pros pp. 24–26 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Volume I · Source section 89 of 105

S15 | Digital workflows: strengths and limitations

F Pros Chapter 13 → Diploma Unit 11

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 1.9 · 2c.5 · 3a.5

CORE PRINCIPLE

Digital is a method—not proof that the impression, plan or result is accurate.

01 When an intraoral scan helps

Good access and controlled moisture permit rapid review and rescanning, especially for single units and shorter spans. Accuracy depends on visibility, scanner technique, software and surface characteristics.

02 When conventional methods remain useful

Full-arch stitching, movable edentulous tissues, functional impressions, subgingival bleeding margins and multiple-implant passive fit can create limitations. Use a validated technique and verification where indicated.

03 Know the file vocabulary

Trueness means closeness to the reference; precision means repeatability. STL contains surface geometry; DICOM is used for volumetric imaging. Merging scans can support prosthetically led planning, but mismatches must be checked.

04 CAD/CAM options

Milling provides reproducible dense industrial materials but has tool-radius and material-waste limits. Printing is useful for models, trays and provisionals; post-curing and material indication affect outcomes.

05 Records and consent

Use digital design to explain options, not to promise a perfect smile. Save source files securely, document revisions, and check the limits and validation status of the individual device/workflow.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Complex guided implant surgery and advanced computer-assisted rehabilitation belong under appropriately trained services.

Source material: F Pros pp. 37–38 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Edition 2 | Unit 11: Peri-implant mucositis versus peri-implantitis

Peri-implant mucositis versus peri-implantitis

IMPLANTS AND DIGITAL WORKFLOWS

CORE PRINCIPLE

Bleeding and suppuration alone are not enough to diagnose progressive peri-implant bone loss; use probing, baseline radiographs and the course of the disease.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Bleeding on gentle probing; no progressive bone lossPeri-implant mucositis Biofilm control, prosthesis cleansability and re-evaluation
Inflammation plus progressive crestal bone lossPeri-implantitis more likely Determine treatability, disease severity and referral need
Deep sulcus after implantation without reference baselineDifficult to diagnose by probing depth aloneSeek prior records and assess serial imaging/clinical changes
Loose implant crown; normal peri-implant tissuesPossible prosthetic screw complicationDifferentiate component looseness from loss of osseointegration

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The EFP S3 pathway supports supportive peri-implant care and non-surgical biofilm removal for mucositis, with assessment of prosthesis access and risk factors. For peri-implantitis, start with diagnosis and non-surgical treatment, re-evaluate and involve a suitably competent practitioner for advanced treatment where necessary.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A bleeding site around an implant with stable radiographic bone and inadequate floss access is not managed like one with suppuration and increasing radiographic bone loss. In the first, focus on plaque control and cleansability; in the second, investigate disease progression and treatment complexity.

EXAM TRAP

Microbial communities are polymicrobial; no single "peri-implantitis pathogen" explains all presentations.

Edition 2 | Unit 11: The mandibular two-implant overdenture: space and attachments

The mandibular two-implant overdenture: space and attachments

IMPLANTS AND DIGITAL WORKFLOWS

CORE PRINCIPLE

The McGill two-implant mandibular overdenture is an important evidence-based option, but attachment choice follows interarch space, implant position, dexterity and maintenance.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Two parallel interforaminal implants; adequate spaceStud/Locator-type retention may be suitableAssess wear inserts, hygiene, implant divergence and replacement
Two implants with divergence or splinting needBar-clip system may be consideredRequires greater vertical restorative space and access
Limited restorative height under proposed dentureInsufficient space for matrix, acrylic and teethMeasure and redesign before selecting an attachment
Opposing maxillary complete dentureUpper denture stability, wear and load matterConsider occlusion and maxillary support before increasing retention

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Published restorative-space figures vary with attachment family and denture design; they are not universal: verify manufacturer minimum stack height, denture base thickness, teeth clearance, hygiene and repair access. Low-profile studs generally demand less space than many bar assemblies. Implant location and lingual inclination influence the path of insertion and attachment wear.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A severely resorbed mandible has enough room for a low-profile attachment but not a proposed bar with clips, acrylic and teeth. A stud may be the better restoration provided implant alignment, support and maintenance are satisfactory.

EXAM TRAP

"Two implants" is not a mandate for every patient; patient factors, access, cost and anatomy govern consent and selection.

Find the cause before you replace: most failures are retention, caries or fatigue.

IN ONE MINUTE

Repeated decementation → resistance form. Porcelain fracture → unsupported porcelain.

A framework that will not seat → a distorted impression or cast.

Survival (still in place) is not success (free of complications).

When a restoration fails, the exam wants you to find the cause before replacing it: an identical replacement will fail the same

way.

12.3 Complete dentures — maintenance

Recall: at least annually for mucosal examination, fit and occlusal wear.

Reline or rebase when fit is lost but the polished and occlusal surfaces are acceptable; remake when OVD, aesthetics, or occlusion are also wrong.

Repairs: fracture lines must be reassembled accurately before a cast is poured; self-cured acrylic repairs are weaker; investigate the cause of repeated fractures (Section 7.9).

Denture hygiene: brush with a soft brush and soap or non-abrasive cleanser over a basin of water, soak overnight (hypochlorite only for acrylic, no metal), leave out at night.

12.4 Laboratory and external factors

Errors arise at: impressions (distortion, drag, voids), casts (air bubbles, abraded dies), articulation (incorrect records), wax and investment (distortion), casting (porosity, incomplete casting), processing (acrylic porosity, raised OVD from flash), and finishing (over-polished fitting surfaces).

Prevention: clear written prescriptions, quality control at each clinical stage (inspect impressions and casts on return), good communication including photographs and shade, agreed delivery times.

12.5 Assessing outcomes

Compare outcomes with published survival data and with the patient's goals (patient-reported outcomes: comfort, function, aesthetics, satisfaction).

Survival = the prosthesis is still in situ; success = in situ and free of complications. Ask which is reported when interpreting studies.

S16 | Failure analysis and measurable success

F Pros Chapters 5–7 and 11 → Diploma Unit 12

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES 2c.21–2c.27 · 3a.2–3a.8

CORE PRINCIPLE

A sound answer diagnoses why a prosthesis failed before choosing the repair or remake.

01 Diagnose by category

Biological: new caries, pulpal symptoms, periodontal/peri-implant inflammation. Mechanical: fractured tooth/restoration, clasp failure, screw loosening or debond. Functional: occlusal interference, instability or inadequate support.

02 Review the sequence of failure

Ask when symptoms began, whether fit/occlusion altered, whether maintenance occurred and whether risk factors changed. Use history, clinical examination, photographs, tests, radiographs and old records as justified.

03 Correct cause—not appearance

An RPD repeatedly fracturing may reflect inadequate thickness, support or occlusal forces. A debonding crown may signal poor retention form. Excess cement, inaccessible hygiene and design can underlie peri-implant inflammation.

04 Audit outcomes

Document comfort, function, aesthetics, cleaning, biological health, mechanical integrity and patient satisfaction. Survival percentages alone do not capture complications or burden of maintenance.

05 Feedback to the plan

Treat failure as an opportunity to change the design, risk control, consent or review interval. Escalate repeated complex failures or combined specialist problems beyond Level 2 competence.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Case-based reasoning and honest complication communication are more important than memorising unsupported survival figures.

Source material: F Pros pp. 20, 22–26, 33–34 · Cross-checked against Diploma learning outcomes (Aug 2026)

Edition 2 | Unit 12: Failure analysis: diagnose before remake

Failure analysis: diagnose before remake

COMPLICATIONS AND MAINTENANCE

CORE PRINCIPLE

A repeat complication is a test of the original design hypothesis. Recreating the same prosthesis without identifying the cause is rarely sound management.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Crown repeatedly decements Lack of resistance, short axial walls or occlusal overloadAssess prep geometry, fit, caries and path of insertion
Upper denture fractures at midline repeatedlyFatigue, flexure or stress concentrationsReview fitting surface, antagonist, occlusion and section thickness
RPD clasps deform or loosen Over-deflection, poor reciprocation or changing supportResurvey, check base fit, support and abutment prognosis
Overdenture insert wears rapidlyImplant divergence, seating errors or excessive retentionCheck attachment alignment, maintenance and occlusal load

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Use a structured failure review: diagnosis, sequence of events, tissue/tooth status, prosthesis design, material defect, function, patient factors, cost and alternatives. Separate biological complications from mechanical and aesthetic failures; some require referral and others simple maintenance.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

An upper complete denture fractures again after two cold-cure repairs and repeated occlusal adjustments. The best step is a comprehensive support/occlusal design review, potentially a remake - not simply stronger cement or more autopolymerising acrylic.

EXAM TRAP

A repair without patient-centred discussion of recurrence risk and follow-up is an incomplete treatment plan.
