Unit 13: Governance and communication

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 50

Montgomery for consent, the MCA for capacity, candour when things go wrong, and adult records kept 11 years.

IN ONE MINUTE

GDC: nine principles; enhanced CPD 100 hours in 5 years.

IR(ME)R duty holders and HTM 01-05 decontamination.

Safeguarding: record and refer; never investigate yourself.

These are the most learnable marks in the paper: the answers follow UK law and GDC standards, not opinion. The rules below are for England unless stated; check devolved-nation equivalents.

13.1 Consent and capacity

Valid consent is informed, voluntary, given by a person with capacity, and specific to the treatment; it is a process,

documented in the notes, and can be withdrawn at any time.

Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015): the clinician must disclose material risks — those a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider significant, or that this particular patient would — and reasonable alternatives (including no treatment).

It replaced Bolam as the test for disclosure.

Bolam (1957): standard of care is that of a responsible body of professional opinion; Bolitho (1997): that opinion must withstand logical analysis. Both still apply to diagnosis and treatment (not disclosure).

Negligence requires duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting harm. Vicarious liability: an employer is liable for the acts of employees in the course of employment.

Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) principles: presume capacity; take all practicable steps to help the person decide; an unwise decision does not mean incapacity; act in best interests; choose the least restrictive option. Two-stage test: impairment of mind or brain, then can the person understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision? Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.

Scotland: Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000.

Young people: 16–17-year-olds are presumed to have capacity to consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969); under 16s may consent if Gillick competent.

Shared decision-making (NICE NG197): discuss benefits, risks, alternatives and doing nothing (BRAN); use decision aids; check understanding.

13.2 GDC Standards for the Dental Team — nine principles

Put patients' interests first.

Communicate effectively with patients.

Obtain valid consent.

Maintain and protect patients' information.

Have a clear and effective complaints procedure.

Work with colleagues in a way that is in patients' best interests.

Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills.

Raise concerns if patients are at risk.

Make sure your personal behaviour maintains patients' confidence in you and the dental profession.

Volume I · Source section 98 of 105

Unit 13: Governance and communication

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 51

Enhanced CPD (dentists): at least 100 verifiable hours per 5-year cycle, at least 10 hours in every 2-year period, with a personal development plan; recommended topics include medical emergencies, decontamination, radiography and radiation protection, legal and ethical issues, complaints handling, oral cancer detection, safeguarding.

Appropriate indemnity is mandatory.

13.3 Duty of candour, incidents and complaints

Professional duty of candour (all registrants): be open and honest when something goes wrong, apologise, offer an appropriate remedy, explain the short- and long-term effects. Statutory duty of candour applies to CQC-registered providers for notifiable safety incidents. An apology is not an admission of liability.

Incident reporting: significant event analysis and root cause analysis locally; NHS patient safety events to the national system

(Learn from Patient Safety Events); adverse drug reactions via MHRA Yellow Card; medical device incidents to MHRA; serious

workplace injuries and dangerous occurrences under RIDDOR to the HSE.

Never events are wholly preventable serious incidents (e.g., wrong-site surgery including wrong tooth extraction).

NHS complaints (England): acknowledge within 3 working days; resolve locally; complaint normally made within 12 months of

the event or of becoming aware; escalation to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Private patients: the Dental

Complaints Service. Respond in writing, apologise where appropriate, explain, and describe actions taken.

Raising concerns (whistleblowing) is protected by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; GDC requires registrants to raise

concerns even if they are not the employer.

13.4 Records and information governance

Records must be accurate, contemporaneous, legible, attributable, and never altered without a dated, signed note of the change.

Retention (NHS England guidance): adults at least 11 years after the last treatment; children until age 25 or 11 years after the

last treatment, whichever is longer. Radiographs and models are part of the record.

UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018: lawful basis for processing, security, data minimisation. Subject access requests answered within one month, normally free of charge. Caldicott principles govern confidential information sharing.

Confidentiality may be breached with consent, when required by law (court order), or in the public interest (serious harm to others) — share the minimum necessary.

13.5 Radiation protection

IRR17 (Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017): protect workers and public; employer registers with the HSE, appoints a

radiation protection adviser (RPA) and radiation protection supervisor (RPS), sets local rules and a controlled area (for intraoral sets, typically within 1.5 m of the tube and patient and within the primary beam until attenuated).

IR(ME)R 2017: protect patients; duty holders are employer, referrer, practitioner (justifies) and operator; justification,

optimisation (ALARP), clinical evaluation and recording of every exposure; pregnancy enquiries where relevant.

Optimisation tools: rectangular collimation, film holders, fastest image receptor, appropriate kV and exposure, quality

assurance programme and audit of image quality.

13.6 Infection prevention and control (HTM 01-05)

Decontamination cycle

Transport → Cleaning → Inspection → Sterilisation → Storage → Use

Cleaning: washer-disinfector is best practice; ultrasonic or manual acceptable for essential quality. Inspection under illuminated magnification.

Steam sterilisation at 134–137°C for at least 3 minutes. Vacuum (type B) sterilisers are needed for wrapped and hollow or lumened instruments; non-vacuum (type N) for unwrapped solid instruments.

Daily automatic control test (and steam penetration test for vacuum sterilisers); periodic testing and validation by a competent

Volume I · Source section 99 of 105

Unit 13: Governance and communication

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 52

person.

Separate dirty-to-clean workflow; ideally a dedicated decontamination room.

Prosthodontic items: rinse and disinfect impressions, records, try-ins and appliances before they go to or come back from the laboratory; label as disinfected.

Dental unit waterlines: flush at the start of the day (about 2 minutes) and between patients (20–30 seconds); use biocide; test microbial quality.

Sharps injury: encourage bleeding, wash with soap and water (no scrubbing), cover, report, contact occupational health urgently (HIV post-exposure prophylaxis ideally within 1 hour, up to 72 hours); assess source patient risk with consent.

Hepatitis B vaccination with documented response for exposure-prone procedures.

13.7 Safeguarding, equality and diversity

Safeguarding children and adults at risk: recognise (injuries to head, face and mouth; dental neglect; unusual behaviour), record, refer (practice safeguarding lead, local authority children's or adult social care; police if immediate danger). Do not investigate yourself; information sharing to protect a child or adult is lawful.

Female genital mutilation: regulated health professionals in England and Wales must report known cases in under-18s to the police.

Equality Act 2010: nine protected characteristics (age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership,

pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation); duty to make reasonable adjustments (e.g., wheelchair access, longer appointments, easy-read information).

13.8 Clinical governance, audit and evidence

Pillars: clinical effectiveness and audit, risk management, education and training, patient and public involvement, information

management, staff management, research.

Audit cycle

Choose topic → Set standard → Measure current practice → Compare with standard → Implement change →

Re-audit (closes the loop)

Audit measures practice against a standard; research generates new knowledge; service evaluation describes current service without a standard.

Quality improvement: Plan–Do–Study–Act cycles, run charts, root cause analysis, significant event analysis, human factors, checklists (e.g., local safety standards for invasive procedures).

Hierarchy of evidence: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs → RCT → cohort → case–control → case series and reports → expert opinion. GRADE rates certainty of evidence.

Key statistics: sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate); positive predictive value depends on prevalence; number needed to treat = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction; a 95% confidence interval crossing 1 (for ratios) or 0 (for differences) is not statistically significant.

Regulators of services: CQC (England), Healthcare Improvement Scotland, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, RQIA (Northern

Ireland). Professional regulator: GDC.

Level 2 practitioners must have a formal link with a consultant-led managed clinical network, complete a minimum caseload,

record outcomes (PROMs and PREMs), audit, and report complications.

13.9 Communication

Breaking bad news (SPIKES): Setting, Perception (what do they know?), Invitation (how much do they want to know?),

Knowledge (warning shot, plain language, small chunks), Emotions (acknowledge and empathise), Strategy and Summary.

Language barriers: professional interpreter, not family members or children.

Hearing impairment: face the patient, remove mask when safe, written information, BSL interpreter. Learning disability: easy-

read and Makaton, involve carers, longer appointments. Dementia: short simple choices, consistent clinician and environment.

Volume I · Source section 100 of 105

Unit 13: Governance and communication

Clean-source transcription · Original notebook p. 53

Children: age-appropriate language, tell–show–do, involve parents.

Referral letters: patient details, reason for referral and question to answer, relevant history, medications, findings, radiographs, urgency, patient's wishes; copy to the patient where appropriate.

Written treatment plans and estimates (NHS FP17DC in England) support informed consent and reduce complaints.

Examiner traps — Unit 13

An apology is not an admission of liability.

16- and 17-year-olds are presumed to have capacity; under-16s need Gillick competence.

Audit measures practice against a standard; research creates new knowledge.

Extracting the wrong tooth is a never event.

Edition 2 | Unit 13: Level 2 decisions, consent and escalation

Level 2 decisions, consent and escalation

GOVERNANCE AND COMMUNICATION

CORE PRINCIPLE

The Diploma tests the independent judgement of an enhanced-skills practitioner, not specialist surgery. Defensible care includes knowing when to refer.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
Stable, maintainable prosthesis with local defectA repair or review may have best risk-benefit ratioDiscuss conservative alternatives and monitor
Uncontrolled disease before extensive restorationDefinitive prosthesis is premature Stabilise caries, periodontitis and risk factors first
Complex rehabilitation, advanced perio/implant surgeryOutcome beyond operator competenceRefer with diagnostic records and clear clinical question
Persistent ulcer, progressive neuropathy or airway threatTime-critical red flag Urgent escalation rather than repeated denture adjustment

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

Consent requires an individualised explanation of likely benefit, risks, uncertainty, maintenance, complications, alternatives and the option of no replacement. Record decision capacity, patient priorities and how risks were communicated. Relevant audit outcomes include prosthesis survival, patient-reported function, recalls, repair incidence and clinical stability.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

A patient asks for multiple implants despite active Stage IV periodontitis and poor attendance. A specialist referral and disease-control sequence is more defensible than immediate implant surgery even if the procedure is technically possible.

EXAM TRAP

Passing an examination does not replace local credentialing or establish competence to undertake every Level 2 procedure.

S17 | Final-week integrated decision traps

F Pros crash notebook → Diploma Unit 14

DIPLOMA LEARNING OUTCOMES Across 1, 2a, 2b, 2c and 3a–3b

CORE PRINCIPLE

Use these prompts to test the decisions common to both source notebooks—not as official examination predictions.

01 Diagnose before intervening

A suspicious lesion needs investigation/referral, not camouflage by a prosthesis. In ambiguous test results, repeat or complement the clinical examination instead of forcing a diagnosis.

02 Stabilise and preserve

Caries/periodontal control precedes complex definitive work. Prefer additive or reversible approaches where they meet the need; no treatment is a legitimate comparator for a missing tooth.

03 Design with forces in mind

RPD support precedes clasp selection; a distal extension needs indirect retention and maintenance. Low denture retention can be functional-border failure rather than an adhesive deficiency.

04 Material chemistry matters

A post retains, not reinforces. Silane is for suitable silica-based surfaces, not zirconia. Good cement cannot rescue a short and severely over-tapered preparation.

05 Recognise your level

Routine Level 2 planning may include moderately difficult tooth replacement; complex multidisciplinary care, severe parafunction, full-mouth reorganisation, complex implants and specialist trauma management need escalation.

06 Answer the clinical question asked

Look for “first,” “most appropriate” or “least invasive,” and select the patient-safe next action rather than the most sophisticated possible procedure.

SCOPE / GUIDANCE

Revision prompts are educational summaries of the supplied notes; exact standards and medications require current verification.

Numbers are conditional: SBA crosswalk and evidence

HIGH-YIELD REVISION

CORE PRINCIPLE

Treat measurement values as decision aids. Always ask what material, patient, laboratory system and measurement method produced the number.

Finding → mechanism → defensible action

Clinical findingInterpretation / mechanismPreferred next action
0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 mm survey gaugesMeasure retentive undercuts, not automatic clasp prescriptionsCross-check material modulus, geometry, abutment and path
2-4 mm freeway space; varying individual valuesA jaw relation cross-check, not a fixed endpointCorrelate speech, facial support, comfort and repeatability
Crown/ceramic reduction valuesDepend on material and manufacturerCheck required bulk, ferrule and resistance form
Implant attachment vertical heightDepends on components plus denture thicknessMeasure available interarch distance before selecting system

CLINICAL DISCRIMINATOR

The updated Volume II SBA bank is 1,500 questions: 270 Foundation, 730 Intermediate and 500 Advanced. Filter by Block A for applied anatomy, B pathology, C materials, D medical, E assessment, F RPD, G complete dentures, H fixed, I occlusion, J failing dentition, K implants, L maintenance, M governance; Block N is integrated cases. Advanced questions are dispersed across their clinical blocks, so the original source's Q1001-Q2000 block numbering is obsolete.

CASE CONTRAST / NEAR MISS

In an SBA, a numerical choice is strong only when the stem supplies the missing constraints. A 0.5-mm undercut plus a short Co-Cr clasp cannot be answered by a memorised "gold clasp" association without checking geometry.

EXAM TRAP

Cited source tags on new pages: LO learning outcomes; NH Level 2 standards; RC RCSEd exam; BSP classification; EFP periodontal care; IM peri-implant guideline; IADT trauma; SD drug prescribing; MC overdenture consensus; M original notes.
